column28: explanation

column9: Match each pedigree symbol to what it means.
column16: Completely shaded symbol :: Affected (shows the trait)
column17: Half-shaded symbol, or a dot in the center :: Carrier (has one copy but doesn't show it)
column28: Squares are males and circles are females. A completely shaded symbol means the person is affected (shows the trait). A half-shaded symbol, or a dot in the center, marks a carrier, and a slash through a symbol means the person has died.
column29: Sort the symbols into groups first: two of them tell you whether a person is male or female, and the rest are marks that tell you about the trait or about the person.

column9: Match each part of a pedigree to what it shows.
column14: Horizontal line joining a square and a circle :: Partners (a mating pair)
column15: Vertical line dropping down from the middle of a horizontal line :: Leads to a couple's children
column16: Horizontal bar with several symbols hanging below it :: Brothers and sisters
column17: Roman numerals (I, II, III) down the left side :: Generations
column18: Symbol farthest to the left on a bar of hanging symbols :: The oldest child
column28: A horizontal line joining a square and a circle shows partners (a mating pair), and a vertical line drops from the middle of it to the couple's children. Brothers and sisters all hang from one horizontal bar (the sibship line), with the oldest on the left. Roman numerals number the generations, with the oldest generation at the top.
column29: Side-by-side lines connect people in the same generation; up-and-down lines connect one generation to the next.

column9: Mendel learned how traits are inherited by crossing pea plants on purpose. Why do scientists use **pedigrees** to study inheritance in humans instead?
column14: Human genes don't follow the same rules as pea plant genes
column15: Scientists can't plan human crosses, and families are small
column16: Punnett squares only work for plants, not for people
column17: Most human traits are carried on the X chromosome
column28: Scientists can't choose which people have children together, families have only a few children, and a human generation takes about 20–30 years. So instead of planned crosses, they look back at the matings that already happened in a family. Human genes follow the same dominant and recessive rules as pea plants, Punnett squares work for people too (you use them with pedigrees), and most human genes are on autosomes, not the X.
column29: Think about how Mendel got his data: he chose which plants to cross and grew hundreds of offspring. Could anyone do that with people?

column9: What is a pedigree?
column14: A chart of a person's blood type and antibodies
column15: A picture of all of a person's chromosomes, in pairs
column16: A grid showing the possible offspring from one cross
column17: A family tree that tracks one trait through several generations
column28: A pedigree is a family tree for a single trait: it shows who has the trait and how it passes from parents to children over several generations. A picture of chromosomes is a karyotype, and the grid for one cross is a Punnett square.
column29: Pedigrees are drawn with squares, circles, and lines that connect them. What do those shapes and lines stand for?

column9: In a pedigree, a completely shaded square stands for a male who shows (is affected by) the trait.
column28: True. Square = male, and complete shading = affected. An unshaded square would be an unaffected male.
column29: What does the shape tell you, and what does the shading tell you?

column9: In a pedigree, what does the label **II-3** mean?
column14: The third person from the left in generation II
column15: The second person from the left in generation III
column16: A person with two affected parents and three children
column17: The third generation of a family with two children
column28: The Roman numeral is the generation (II = the second generation), and the number after the dash counts people from left to right in that row. So II-3 is the third person from the left in generation II. III-2 would be the second person in generation III.
column29: Roman numeral first, then a regular number. Which one is the row (generation)?

column9: A trait shows up in a grandfather and in one of his grandchildren, but in no one in the generation between them. What kind of trait is it most likely to be?
column28: Skipping a generation is the sign of a recessive trait: the middle generation carried the allele (Aa) without showing it. A dominant trait shows up in every generation, because anyone with the allele shows it.
column29: Can a trait hide in a person who doesn't show it? Which kind of allele can hide?

column9: In a pedigree for an **autosomal** trait, two unaffected parents have an affected child. What does this tell you about the trait?
column14: The trait is dominant, and both parents are heterozygous
column15: The trait is recessive, and only one parent is a carrier
column16: The trait is dominant, and one parent is homozygous
column17: The trait is recessive, and both parents are carriers
column28: Neither parent shows the trait, but their child does, so the allele was hiding in the parents: the trait must be recessive. The affected child is aa and got an a from each parent, so both parents are carriers (Aa × Aa); one carrier parent couldn't give the child two a's. If the trait were dominant, the child's A would have to come from a parent, and any parent with an A would show the trait.
column29: The child got one allele from each parent. What did each parent have to give, and could they give it without showing the trait?

column9: In a pedigree, almost all of the affected people are males. Which inheritance pattern is most likely?
column28: X-linked recessive traits affect mostly males, because males have only one X, so one recessive allele is enough. A female needs two copies, which is much less likely. X-linked dominant traits show up in more females than males (females have two X's that could carry the allele), and autosomal traits affect males and females about equally.
column29: Which chromosome do males have only one copy of?

column9: An autosomal trait (one whose gene is on chromosomes 1–22) affects males and females at about the same rate.
column28: True. Males and females have the same autosomes, so autosomal traits show up in both sexes about equally. Among the patterns in this unit, a big difference between males and females points to a sex-linked (X-linked) trait.
column29: Do males and females have the same autosomes?

column9: In a pedigree for an autosomal recessive trait, every affected (shaded) person has the genotype ___. Use **A** and **a**.
column28: A recessive trait only shows with two recessive alleles, so every affected person is aa. Unaffected people are AA or Aa.
column29: How many recessive alleles does it take to show a recessive trait?

column9: Maddie is a **carrier** of albinism, an autosomal recessive trait. Which statement describes her?
column14: She is Aa, and she does not have albinism
column15: She is aa, and she does not have albinism
column16: She is Aa, and her skin is slightly lighter than normal
column17: She is AA, and she does not have albinism
column28: A carrier is heterozygous (Aa): she has one recessive allele that she can pass on, but her dominant A hides it, so she does not have albinism and looks just like someone who is AA. A person who is aa would have albinism, and someone who is AA has no recessive allele to carry.
column29: What does a carrier 'carry'? How many copies of a recessive allele does it take for the trait to show?

column9: Which of these is an example of an **autosomal dominant** disorder?
column28: Huntington's disease is autosomal dominant: one copy of the allele causes it. Cystic fibrosis and sickle cell anemia are autosomal recessive, and hemophilia is X-linked recessive.
column29: Two of these need two copies of the allele, and one is on the X chromosome.

column9: For which inheritance pattern can an affected father **never** pass the trait to his son?
column17: It can pass from father to son in every pattern
column28: A father gives his Y chromosome, not his X, to his sons, so an X-linked allele from the father can't reach a son. Autosomal traits can pass from father to son, because fathers and sons share the same autosomes.
column29: Which sex chromosome does a father give to his son?

column9: For an autosomal dominant trait, every affected person has at least one affected parent.
column28: True. A dominant allele can't hide, so the parent who passed it on also shows the trait. That's why autosomal dominant traits appear in every generation.
column29: Can a dominant allele hide in a parent who doesn't show it?

column9:
**Pedigree:**
Generation I: I-1 (unaffected male) and I-2 (unaffected female) are partners.
Generation II (their children): II-1 (affected female), II-2 (unaffected male), II-3 (unaffected female)
Which inheritance pattern fits this pedigree?
column28: Two unaffected parents have an affected child, so the trait is recessive. It can't be X-linked recessive, because an affected daughter (X^{a}X^{a}) would need an affected father, and I-1 is unaffected. That leaves autosomal recessive, with both parents carriers (Aa × Aa). Dominant patterns are out because a dominant trait can't hide in both parents.
column29: First ask: do two unaffected parents have an affected child? Then check the affected daughter's father.

column9:
**Pedigree:**
Generation I: I-1 (affected male) and I-2 (affected female) are partners.
Generation II (their children): II-1 (unaffected female), II-2 (affected male), II-3 (affected female)
Which inheritance pattern fits this pedigree?
column28: Two affected parents have an unaffected child. That can only happen if the trait is dominant and both parents are heterozygous (Aa × Aa → 25% aa). If it were recessive, two affected (aa) parents could only have affected children; that rules out both recessive patterns. X-linked dominant is out because an affected father would pass the trait to every daughter, but II-1 is unaffected.
column29: Could two affected parents have an unaffected child if the trait were recessive?

column9:
**Pedigree:** The trait is rare.
Generation I: I-1 (unaffected male) and I-2 (unaffected female) are partners.
Generation II (their children): II-1 (affected male), II-2 (unaffected female), II-4 (affected male), II-5 (unaffected female)
II-2's partner: II-3 (unaffected male, married in)
Generation III (children of II-2 and II-3): III-1 (affected male), III-2 (unaffected female)
Which inheritance pattern is most likely?
column28: Only males are affected, the trait skips generations, and it passes from unaffected (carrier) mothers to their sons: I-2 to II-1 and II-4, then II-2 to III-1. That's the X-linked recessive pattern. It isn't dominant, because unaffected parents have affected children. Autosomal recessive would need the married-in man II-3 to be a carrier too, which is unlikely for a rare trait, and it wouldn't explain why only males are affected.
column29: Who is affected: males, females, or both? And which parents passed the trait on?

column9: An autosomal recessive trait shows up in II-2. His father, I-1, is **affected**, and his mother, I-2, is unaffected. What are the genotypes of I-1 and I-2?
column28: In a recessive pedigree, every affected person is aa, so I-1 is aa. II-2 is affected too, so he got an a from each parent, including his mother. I-2 doesn't show the trait, so her other allele is A: she is Aa. AA couldn't give II-2 an a, Aa and Aa would leave I-1 unaffected, and AA is never the genotype of an affected person in a recessive pedigree.
column29: Start with the affected people: what genotype do they have? Then ask what II-2 had to get from his mother.

column9: In a pedigree, II-3 and II-4 are both carriers (**Aa**) of an autosomal recessive trait. What is the chance that their next child will be affected? Answer in %, as a number like 80.
column28: Punnett square: Aa × Aa → AA, Aa, Aa, aa. Only aa is affected: 1 of 4 boxes = 25%. The other three boxes (AA, Aa, Aa) are unaffected.
column29: An affected child must be aa. How many of the 4 boxes are aa?

column9: Jacob's parents are both carriers of cystic fibrosis, an autosomal recessive disorder (**Aa × Aa**). What is the chance that a child of theirs will be a **carrier**, like them? Answer in %, as a number like 80.
column28: Punnett square: Aa × Aa → AA, Aa, Aa, aa. Carriers are Aa: 2 of 4 boxes = 50%. The AA box is not a carrier, and the aa box is affected.
column29: Count only the boxes with one A and one a.

column9: Huntington's disease is autosomal dominant. A man with Huntington's who is heterozygous (**Aa**) has children with a woman who does not have it (**aa**). What is the chance that each child will have Huntington's? Answer in %, as a number like 80.
column28: Punnett square: Aa × aa → Aa, Aa, aa, aa. The Aa children have the disorder, because one dominant allele is enough: 2 of 4 boxes = 50%. So each child of a heterozygous affected parent and an unaffected parent has a 50% chance of having Huntington's.
column29: With a dominant disorder, how many copies of A does it take to be affected?

column9: In an autosomal **dominant** pedigree, what is the genotype of every **unaffected** person?
column28: If the trait is dominant, anyone with even one A shows it. So unaffected people can't have any A: they are all aa. Affected people are AA or Aa.
column29: For a dominant trait, how many A alleles can an unaffected person have?

column9: In an autosomal dominant pedigree, II-2 is affected, and one of her children (III-1) is unaffected. II-2's genotype must be ___. Use **A** and **a**.
column28: III-1 is unaffected, so III-1 is aa and got an a from II-2. II-2 is affected, so she also has an A. Her genotype must be Aa. If she were AA, every child would get an A and be affected.
column29: The unaffected child is aa. What did II-2 have to pass on to that child?

column9: Why does an autosomal dominant trait usually **not** skip a generation?
column14: Two copies of a dominant allele are needed to show it
column15: Dominant alleles are passed to sons more than daughters
column16: Dominant alleles are more common than recessive ones
column17: One copy shows the trait, so it can't hide in a parent
column28: One copy of a dominant allele is enough to show the trait, so it can't hide in a carrier. A child can only get it from a parent who shows it, which is why it appears in every generation. One copy (not two) is enough, autosomal dominant alleles pass to sons and daughters equally, and dominant alleles aren't necessarily common (Huntington's is rare).
column29: Can a person have a dominant allele and not show it?

column9: Hemophilia is X-linked recessive. Priya does not have hemophilia, but her father does. What is Priya's genotype?
column28: A father gives his only X to every daughter. Priya's father has hemophilia (X^{h}Y), so she got X^{h} from him. She doesn't have hemophilia, so her other X must be X^{H}: she is a carrier, X^{H}X^{h}. X^{h}X^{h} would give her hemophilia, and X^{H}Y is a male genotype.
column29: Which X does every daughter get from her father?

column9: Which clues point to an **autosomal recessive** pattern in a pedigree? Select all that apply.
column14: Two unaffected parents have an affected child.
column16: Males and females are affected about equally.
column17: Every affected person has an affected parent.
column28: Recessive traits can hide in carriers, so they skip generations and can appear in children of two unaffected parents. Being autosomal means males and females are affected about equally. 'Every affected person has an affected parent' points to dominant, and 'only males are affected' points to X-linked.
column29: Ask yourself two questions: what can a recessive allele do that a dominant allele can't, and what does being on an autosome (not the X) mean for which sexes get the trait?

column9: When you write genotypes for a pedigree, what does a **?** in a genotype like **A?** mean?
column14: The second allele can't be figured out from the pedigree
column15: The person is a carrier of the recessive allele
column16: It isn't known whether the person shows the trait
column28: A ? stands for an allele you can't determine from the pedigree: the person could have either allele, so you write the one you know for sure and a ? for the other. A carrier you can prove would be written Aa, and someone you can prove is AA would be written AA. The ? is never about whether the person shows the trait: the shading already shows that.
column29: Think about an unaffected person in a recessive pedigree. Which genotypes could they have, and can you always tell which one it is?

column9:
**Pedigree:** The trait is autosomal recessive.
Generation I: I-1 (unaffected male) and I-2 (unaffected female) are partners.
Generation II (their children): II-1 (affected male), II-2 (unaffected female)
What genotype should be written for II-2?
column28: II-2 is unaffected, so she has at least one A. Her parents are both Aa (they had an affected son), so she could be AA or Aa, and the pedigree can't tell which. Writing A? shows that the second allele is unknown. aa would make her affected.
column29: Is there anything in the pedigree that proves whether II-2's second allele is A or a?

column9: An X-linked recessive trait runs in a family. A carrier mother (X^{A}X^{a}) and an unaffected father (X^{A}Y) are expecting a son. What is the chance that their son will be affected? Answer in %, as a number like 80.
column28: Punnett square: X^{A}X^{a} × X^{A}Y → sons X^{A}Y and X^{a}Y. Sons get their X from their mother, so half of the sons (50%) are expected to be affected.
column29: Sons get their X from their mother. What two X's can she give?

column9: In a pedigree, a horizontal line connects I-1 (a square) and I-2 (a circle). A vertical line drops from the middle of that line to a horizontal bar. II-1 (a circle), II-2 (a square), and II-3 (a circle) hang from that bar. Which statement is correct?
column14: I-1 and I-2 are brother and sister, and II-2 is their only son
column15: II-1 and II-2 are partners, and I-1 and I-2 are their parents
column16: I-1 and I-2 are partners, and II-1, II-2, and II-3 are their grandchildren
column17: II-2 is the son of I-1 and I-2, and II-1 and II-3 are his sisters
column28: The horizontal line joins I-1 and I-2 as partners, and the vertical line drops to their children, who all hang from one sibship bar. II-2 is a square, so he is their son, and II-1 and II-3 are circles, so they are his sisters. Children on the same sibship bar are siblings, not partners, and generation II is one step below generation I, so its members are children, not grandchildren.
column29: Read the shapes first: who is male and who is female? Then read the lines: who is in the same row, and which row is one generation down?

column9:
**Pedigree:**
Generation I: I-1 (affected male) and I-2 (unaffected female) are partners.
Generation II (their children): II-1 (unaffected male), II-3 (affected female)
II-1's partner: II-2 (unaffected female, married in)
II-3's partner: II-4 (unaffected male, married in)
Generation III: III-1 (affected male) is the child of II-1 and II-2. III-2 (unaffected male) and III-3 (affected male) are the children of II-3 and II-4.
Which person, together with his or her parents, proves that the trait **cannot** be autosomal dominant?
column28: III-1 is affected, but both of his parents (II-1 and II-2) are unaffected. A dominant allele can't hide, so an affected child would need an affected parent; the trait must be recessive. The others fit a dominant trait: II-3 and III-3 are affected children of an affected parent, and III-2 is an unaffected child of an affected mother, which happens when she is Aa.
column29: For each choice, look at that person and his or her parents. Which one could not happen if a single copy of the allele always shows?

column9: Two carriers (**Aa × Aa**) of an autosomal recessive trait already have three unaffected children. The chance that their fourth child will be affected is **higher** than it was for their first child.
column28: False. Each child gets a brand-new combination of alleles: every egg and sperm is a fresh draw, and earlier children don't change which alleles the next child gets. So every child of Aa × Aa parents has the same chance of being aa, no matter how many unaffected children came before. Like a coin, the Punnett square doesn't remember earlier results.
column29: Does an egg or a sperm 'know' which alleles the couple's earlier children got?

column9: Why would a genetic counselor draw a pedigree for a family?
column14: To count the chromosomes in each family member's cells
column15: To change which alleles a future child will inherit
column16: To find out a baby's blood type without a blood test
column17: To estimate the chance that a future child will inherit a condition
column28: Genetic counselors use pedigrees to find the inheritance pattern, spot carriers, and estimate the chance that a future child will inherit a condition. A pedigree can't change alleles, can't replace a blood test, and doesn't show chromosomes (a karyotype does).
column29: A pedigree looks back at a family to make a prediction about what?

column9: Put the steps for using a pedigree to predict the chance of an affected child in order.
column14: Set up a Punnett square for the couple you are asked about.
column15: Decide the inheritance pattern (dominant or recessive, autosomal or X-linked).
column16: Count the boxes to find the chance for the next child.
column17: Write the genotypes of the affected people.
column18: Use parents and children to fill in the other genotypes, writing ? for any allele you can't determine.
column28: You need the pattern before you can write any genotypes. Affected people are the easiest to write (for example, aa in a recessive pedigree), and then their parents and children help fill in everyone else. Only then can you set up the Punnett square for the couple and count the boxes.
column29: You can't write genotypes until you know whether the trait is dominant or recessive.

column9:
**Pedigree:**
Generation I: I-1 (unaffected male) and I-2 (unaffected female) are partners.
Generation II (their children): II-1 (unaffected female), II-3 (affected male)
II-1's partner: II-2 (unaffected male, married in)
II-3's partner: II-4 (unaffected female, married in)
Generation III: III-1 (affected female) and III-2 (affected male) are the children of II-1 and II-2. III-3 (unaffected male) and III-4 (unaffected female) are the children of II-3 and II-4.
Which person shows that the trait **cannot** be X-linked recessive?
column28: For X-linked recessive, III-1 would be X^{a}X^{a}, with one X^{a} from each parent. But her father, II-2, is unaffected (X^{A}Y), so he has no X^{a} to give her. The others fit X-linked recessive: III-2 is an affected son who could get X^{a} from a carrier mother (II-1), III-3 got a Y (not an X) from his affected father, and III-4 can be an unaffected carrier who got X^{a} from her father.
column29: For each choice, write the genotypes X-linked recessive would need for that person and his or her parents. Which one is impossible?

column9:
**Pedigree:**
Generation I: I-1 (affected male) and I-2 (unaffected female) are partners.
Generation II: their daughter II-1 (unaffected female) and her partner II-2 (unaffected male, married in)
Generation III (children of II-1 and II-2): III-1 (affected female), III-2 (unaffected male), III-3 (unaffected female)
Which inheritance pattern fits this pedigree?
column28: The trait skips generation II, and III-1 is affected even though both of her parents are unaffected, so it's recessive. It can't be X-linked recessive, because III-1 is an affected daughter with an unaffected father (II-2). That leaves autosomal recessive: II-1 is a carrier (Aa) who got an a from her father, and II-2 must also be a carrier. (X-linked dominant is out too: affected I-1 would have passed it to his daughter II-1.)
column29: Does the trait skip a generation? Then look at III-1: is her father affected?

column9:
**Pedigree:** The trait is rare.
Generation I: I-1 (affected male) and I-2 (unaffected female) are partners.
Generation II (their children): II-1 (affected female), II-3 (unaffected male), II-4 (affected male)
II-1's partner: II-2 (unaffected male, married in)
II-4's partner: II-5 (unaffected female, married in)
Generation III: III-1 (affected male) and III-2 (unaffected female) are the children of II-1 and II-2. III-3 (affected female) and III-4 (unaffected male) are the children of II-4 and II-5.
Which inheritance pattern is most likely?
column28: The trait appears in every generation, every affected child has an affected parent, and males and females are both affected: the autosomal dominant fingerprint. A recessive pattern would need I-2, II-2, and II-5 (all unaffected) to carry a rare allele, which is very unlikely. X-linked dominant is impossible, because II-4 is an affected son whose only X came from his unaffected mother. X-linked recessive would need I-2 to be a carrier and the married-in II-5 to be a carrier too (for their affected daughter III-3), which is very unlikely for a rare trait.
column29: Does the trait skip any generation? Does every affected person have an affected parent? Does it pass from father to son?

column9:
**Pedigree:** The trait is X-linked recessive.
Generation I: I-1 (affected male) and I-2 (unaffected female) are partners.
Generation II: their son II-1 (unaffected male) and his partner II-2 (unaffected female, married in)
Generation III (children of II-1 and II-2): III-1 (affected male), III-2 (unaffected female)
What is II-2's genotype?
column28: III-1 is an affected son (X^{a}Y), and a son's only X comes from his mother, so II-2 must have an X^{a}. She is unaffected, so her other X is X^{A}: she is a carrier, X^{A}X^{a}. The affected grandfather, I-1, isn't the source: he gave his son II-1 a Y, not his X^{a}, so II-1 is X^{A}Y. X^{a}X^{a} would make II-2 affected, and X^{A}Y is a male genotype.
column29: Where did III-1's only X come from? Could I-1's X^{a} have reached III-1 through II-1?

column9:
**Pedigree:** The trait is autosomal recessive.
Generation II: II-1 (unaffected female) and II-2 (unaffected male) are partners.
Generation III (their children): III-1 (affected male), III-2 (unaffected female)
If II-1 and II-2 have another child, what is the chance that the child will be affected? Answer in %, as a number like 80.
column28: III-1 is affected (aa), so each parent gave him an a. Both parents are unaffected, so both are carriers (Aa). Punnett square: Aa × Aa → AA, Aa, Aa, aa: 1 of 4 boxes is aa = 25%. Having one affected child doesn't change the chance for the next child.
column29: First find II-1's and II-2's genotypes from their affected son, then do the Punnett square.

column9: **Pedigree:** The trait is autosomal recessive. III-2 is affected. She partners with III-5, who is unaffected, but whose mother (II-6) is affected. What is the chance that their first child will be affected? Answer in %, as a number like 80.
column28: III-2 is affected: aa. III-5 is unaffected, but his mother is aa, so she gave him an a: he is Aa. Punnett square: aa × Aa → Aa, Aa, aa, aa: 2 of 4 boxes are aa = 50%.
column29: III-5 doesn't show the trait, but what allele did his affected mother have to give him?

column9: An X-linked recessive trait runs in a family. A carrier mother (X^{A}X^{a}) and an unaffected father (X^{A}Y) are planning another child, and they don't know whether it will be a boy or a girl. What is the chance that the child will be affected? Answer in %, as a number like 80.
column28: Punnett square: X^{A}X^{a} × X^{A}Y → X^{A}X^{A}, X^{A}X^{a}, X^{A}Y, X^{a}Y. Only X^{a}Y is affected: 1 of 4 boxes = 25% of all children. The carrier daughter (X^{A}X^{a}) is unaffected, so she isn't counted.
column29: When the sex of the child is unknown, count all four boxes.

column9: **Pedigree:** The trait is X-linked recessive. II-4 (affected male) partners with II-5 (unaffected female). II-5's father, I-3, is affected. What is the chance that a **daughter** of II-4 and II-5 will be affected? Answer in %, as a number like 80.
column28: II-5 got X^{a} from her affected father, I-3, and she is unaffected, so she is X^{A}X^{a}. II-4 is X^{a}Y. Every daughter gets X^{a} from II-4, and half get X^{a} from II-5: daughters are X^{A}X^{a} (carrier) or X^{a}X^{a} (affected), so 50% of the daughters are expected to be affected.
column29: Find II-5's genotype from her father. Then remember that every daughter gets her father's X.

column9: Storm thinks a trait in her family's pedigree is X-linked recessive. Which observation, if it were in the pedigree, would prove that the trait is **not** X-linked recessive?
column14: An affected woman has an unaffected son
column15: Two unaffected parents have an affected son
column17: An unaffected woman has an affected son
column28: An affected woman is X^{a}X^{a}, so every son gets an X^{a} from her and would be affected. An unaffected son of an affected mother is impossible for X-linked recessive. The other observations all fit X-linked recessive (carrier mothers and skipped generations).
column29: If a woman shows an X-linked recessive trait, which X does every one of her sons get?

column9:
**Pedigree:** The trait is autosomal recessive.
Generation I: I-1 (unaffected male) and I-2 (unaffected female) are partners.
Generation II (their children): II-1 (affected male), II-2 (unaffected male), II-3 (unaffected female)
II-3's partner: II-4 (unaffected male, married in)
Generation III (children of II-3 and II-4): III-1 (affected female), III-2 (unaffected male)
Which people **must** be carriers (**Aa**)? Select all that apply.
